The fundamental epistemic operation described in pages 3 through 5 is the manual discretization of a continuous physical domain into a structured digital ledger. Mathematically, this represents a projection map \Pi: \mathbb{R}^2 \times \mathcal{C} \rightarrow \mathbb{D}, where \mathbb{R}^2 is the bounded Euclidean space of the ice surface defined by the NHL rulebook, \mathcal{C} is the categorical space of game states (Team, Type, Player), and \mathbb{D} is the resulting tabular dataset. The 'click' action serves as a Dirac delta function, collapsing the infinite possibilities of puck/player location into a singular, quantized observation (x, y). 

This manual tracking mechanism inherently introduces a human-in-the-loop measurement error model. Unlike automated optical tracking systems that generate high-frequency trajectories, this web application relies on retrospective or near-real-time human annotation. Consequently, the logged coordinates represent a subjective expectation value of the true event location, heavily influenced by the annotator's cognitive processing speed and visual acuity. The details panel acts as a dynamic constraint solver, ensuring that every spatial point is rigorously bound to a valid semantic context before being committed to the database. 

From a Foundry Sovereign Primitive perspective, this chapter window defines the genesis of the GSI data ontology. It establishes the base layer upon which all higher-order statistical inferences—such as expected goals (xG) models or possession metrics—are built. The explicit mapping of 'Team' to color and 'Type' to shape is not merely a UI choice but a critical encoding of multi-variate features into a visually parsable format, allowing for immediate qualitative pattern recognition before quantitative analysis. The ability to dynamically add types (e.g., 'Traffic') demonstrates a flexible schema capable of evolving with the tactical complexity of the sport, preventing rigid data structures from becoming obsolete.

reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: Modeling the opposing agent—the human tracker—requires understanding their cognitive load and predictive biases. A tracker does not log events purely reactively; they anticipate plays based on team tendencies and player positioning. When a coach deploys a specific forechecking scheme, the tracker's attention shifts, altering the probability distribution of where they will click next. Furthermore, the tracker must infer intent; distinguishing between a 'Shot' and a 'Pass' often relies on micro-cues like stick angle and body orientation. The system effectively externalizes the tracker's internal theory of mind regarding the game, translating their intuitive grasp of hockey physics into structured data points that machines can later process.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: To prevent catastrophic leakage and collinearity in downstream GSE models, strict veto conditions must be applied to this primitive layer. First, temporal aliasing must be monitored; if multiple clicks occur within a timeframe physically impossible for puck travel between the logged coordinates, the data points must be flagged as erroneous or overlapping events. Second, categorical drift must be vetted; if a user arbitrarily creates new 'Type' widgets that semantically overlap with existing ones (e.g., 'Wrist Shot' vs. 'Shot'), it introduces noise that violates the mutual exclusivity assumption required for clean multinomial classification. Finally, spatial outliers that fall exactly on the boundary limits (-100, 42.5) require scrutiny, as true on-ice events rarely occur precisely against the glass at maximum extension, suggesting potential UI clipping errors rather than genuine play.
